name: Margarita
flags: Generic classic cocktail, no source recorded. Family version is a specific house build (3/4 oz lime, 2 oz Espolon Blanco, 1 oz Cointreau, 1/2 oz simple syrup). No published page matches this exact spec and attributing it to any one bartender site would be invention.

name: Marinated Chicken Fingers With Pasta - Franey
flags: Clearly a Pierre Franey NYT 60-Minute Gourmet column (family note says 1992). Searched NYT/pierrefraney.com/general web; the 1992 column is not surfacing online. pierrefraney.com hosts a recipe archive but not this one. Do not substitute an unrelated 'chicken finger pasta'.

name: Meat Loaf with Parsley and Tomato
headnote: A transcription of the Fanny Farmer Cookbook (1986) meat loaf, presented as a base recipe with a set of named variations. The base is a bread-crumb/egg/milk binder with Worcestershire and dry mustard; the 'Parsley and Tomato' variation drops the Worcestershire and mustard, swaps tomato juice for the milk, and folds in minced parsley and crumbled basil, with tomato sauce spooned over the top. The tomato liquid and sauce keep a lean loaf moist while the herbs push it toward an Italian profile. The book suggests turning leftovers into rye-bread sandwiches with pickles.
flags: Confirmed against the family text: 'Meat Loaf with Parsley and Tomato' is the exact name of a variation printed in the Fanny Farmer Cookbook, and the family version is that variation at half scale (1 lb beef, 1 c crumbs, 1 egg, 1/2 onion, 3/8 c tomato sauce, 1/4 c parsley, 1/2 t basil). Source field 'Fannie Farmer' matches. URL is a faithful recipelink.com transcription, not a publisher page; no official Fannie Farmer page exists online.

name: Meatballs
headnote: Blogger Bridget (The Way the Cookie Crumbles) reprints the Cook's Illustrated meatballs, tracing them to the January 1998 issue -- the same recipe collected in The New Best Recipe. The bread-and-buttermilk panade is the point: the soaked paste keeps the meat tender and prevents the dense, bouncy texture that comes from overworking or from dry crumbs. A chuck-and-pork blend plus Parmesan, parsley and an egg yolk supplies fat and flavor, and shallow pan-frying in a quarter-inch of oil browns all sides.
comment_digest: Commenters report reliably tender results. One swapped ground Italian sausage for the pork successfully. A recurring point of confusion is the term 'sweet milk' in the yogurt substitution, which simply means ordinary milk as opposed to buttermilk.
flags: Ingredient list matches the family text essentially line for line, including the unusual 2 slices white bread + 1/2 cup buttermilk panade, 1/4 cup Parmesan, 1 egg yolk, 3/4 tsp salt, and 1-1/4 cups oil for pan-frying. Blog names Cook's Illustrated as the origin, which matches the recorded source 'The New Best Recipe Cookbook'. Runner-up a human might prefer: https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/762-classic-spaghetti-and-meatballs (the publisher's own page, but paywalled).

name: Mushroom Quiche
flags: No source recorded. Family version is distinctive (shallots, 3/4 lb mushrooms, 3 eggs to 1-3/4 c heavy cream, freeze-the-shell step, bake-from-frozen instruction, 170-175F internal temp) and no published recipe matching that ratio or method surfaced. Plenty of generic mushroom quiches exist; none is defensibly this one.

name: Oatmeal Cookies
rating: 31 reviews, Community Pick (no star count displayed)
headnote: A food.com member (spatchcock) posts this as the oatmeal cookie she settled on after testing many others, preferring it because it bakes up crisp rather than cloyingly sweet. It is the older Quaker Oats canister formula, built on shortening or margarine rather than all butter, with a quarter cup of water added to the creamed sugars. That water thins the dough just enough for the three cups of oats to hydrate and spread, which is what gives the crisp edge and chewy center.
comment_digest: The added water is the main argument: one baker regretted it and compensated with extra flour. Several insist the 'optional' salt should be treated as required. Cinnamon, nutmeg, raisins and chocolate chips are all reported as good additions. Pressed into a 9x13 pan for 35-40 minutes it works as a bar cookie. Substituting oil for the shortening gives a crunchier cookie; pulling them at 9-10 minutes instead of the full time gives a chewier one.
flags: Ingredient list matches the family text exactly, including the telltale 3/4 c shortening/margarine, 1/2 c granulated + 1 c brown sugar, 1 egg, and the unusual 1/4 cup water -- this is the pre-1990s Quaker package recipe, consistent with the recorded source 'Quaker Oats 1983'. Marked medium only because this is a member repost on food.com rather than a Quaker-published page; Quaker's current site carries the reformulated all-butter 'Vanishing Oatmeal Raisin Cookies' (1 c butter, 2 eggs, no water), which is NOT the family's version. Runner-up: https://www.justapinch.com/recipes/quakers-best-oatmeal-cookies.html

name: Orange Phyllo Dough Cake (Portokalopita)
flags: Source 'Savor Nafplio' is a cooking class in Nafplio, Greece; the family text is the class handout, with metric weights (700 g sugar syrup, 450 g phyllo, 20 g baking powder). Searched for Savor Nafplio's own publication of it and found nothing. Many published portokalopita recipes exist (My Greek Dish, The Hungry Bites, Mia Kouppa) but none is this class's version and none should be attached.

name: Orange Whip
flags: Family source (Lizzie MacArthur) working from Adelle Davis, Let's Cook It Right. The Adelle Davis Foundation site publishes some of her recipes but not an 'Orange Whip'; the book itself is only on archive.org as a borrowable scan, which is not a citable recipe page.

name: Original Green Bean Casserole
headnote: Campbell's own page for the casserole its test kitchen developed in 1955, still presented as the canonical holiday version. The appeal is the short ingredient list -- condensed cream of mushroom soup, milk, soy sauce, cooked green beans and French fried onions -- assembled in one dish with almost no prep. Holding back two-thirds of the onions and adding them only for the last five minutes is what keeps the topping crisp and golden instead of soggy.
comment_digest: No reader comments on the page. Campbell's own notes cover using fresh blanched, frozen or canned beans interchangeably, and variations with almonds, pancetta or red pepper.
flags: Family text is the Campbell's original verbatim, naming both Campbell's Cream of Mushroom Soup and French's French Fried Onions, with the same 4 c beans / 1-1/3 c onions / 1/2 c milk / 1 t soy sauce proportions and the same two-stage bake (25 min, stir, 5 min). Only drift is the can size (10-3/4 oz in the old printing vs 10.5 oz now).

name: Outdoor Burgers
flags: Family source (Jan Symmes). Confirming search returned only unrelated published burger recipes.

name: Oven-Roasted Rosemary Potatoes
flags: No source recorded. The family text reads like a 1980s Good Housekeeping/Woman's Day clipping ('About 1 1/2 hours before serving', 'salad oil', 5 lb scale, parboil-then-roast at 425). Could not find that clipping. Dozens of unrelated rosemary roasted potato recipes exist online, none of which parboil first at this scale, so none should be attached.

name: Pace Six-Layer Dip
headnote: A member transcription of the Pace Foods promotional recipe, posted to food.com by user kadidel as an easy party dip. It is the layered Tex-Mex dip in its branded form: a bean-dip base, mashed avocado sharpened with lemon juice, a sour cream and mayonnaise layer, then green onions, tomatoes, olives and cheddar, with Pace Picante Sauce spooned over the top. Keeping the avocado under the dairy layer slows browning, and the picante sauce goes on last so it does not soak the base.
flags: Title matches the family entry exactly and the ingredient list is the same recipe, consistent with the recorded source '1985 Pace Foods, Inc.' The family clipping uses can counts (2 cans bean dip, 2 cans olives, 3 tomatoes) where food.com converts to weights (9 oz bean dip, 4 oz olives, 2 tomatoes); otherwise identical. No Pace/Campbell's page for this specific 1985 promo remains online.

name: Parmesan Soup From Elva
flags: Personal source (Elva Adalsteinsdottir). Searching her name with the recipe returns nothing; only unrelated published parmesan soups. Treated as a family/friend recipe.

name: Party Mix
headnote: Chex's own page for the snack mix that made the cereal famous, also known historically as Nuts and Bolts. Three Chex varieties are tossed with melted butter, Worcestershire and seasonings so every piece is coated before baking, which is what dries the cereal to a crisp rather than leaving it greasy. The page gives a fast microwave method and keeps the traditional oven version -- 250F for an hour, stirred every fifteen minutes -- as the alternative.
comment_digest: NO COMMENTS on the brand page. On the food.com transcription of the same recipe (39 reviews) the recurring arguments are that bagel chips and Corn Chex are later additions to what older bakers remember, that the seasonings want doubling, and that cayenne or cheese crackers are worthwhile changes; several recall a 1950s printing that used Cheerios.
flags: Dish identity is certain -- the family text is unmistakably Chex Party Mix (same 6 T butter, 1 1/2 t seasoned salt, 250F for 1 hour stirring every 15 min, spread on absorbent paper to cool). But the family version is an older, smaller printing: 2 cups each of the three Chex rather than 3, 4 t Worcestershire rather than 2 T, garlic SALT rather than garlic powder, no onion powder, no bagel chips, and it adds Cheerios and thin pretzels. No source was recorded in the collection, so this is the canonical brand recipe rather than provably the exact clipping. Runner-up with the oven method foregrounded: https://www.landolakes.com/recipe/9853/the-original-chex-party-mix/

name: Peanut Butter Blossoms
headnote: Pillsbury's page for the cookie as Freda Smith of Gibsonburg, Ohio entered it in the 1957 Bake-Off, where it became one of the contest's most durable recipes. The dough is a soft peanut butter cookie rolled in sugar, and the chocolate kiss goes on only after the cookies come out of the oven so it holds its shape while softening into the still-hot center. That order is the whole trick -- baking the kiss with the cookie melts it flat.
flags: Verified against the family text ingredient by ingredient: 1 3/4 c flour, 1/2 c sugar, 1/2 c brown sugar, 1 t soda, 1/2 t salt, 1/2 c shortening, 1/2 c peanut butter, 2 T milk, 1 t vanilla, 1 egg, roll in sugar, kisses. This is the Pillsbury original, NOT the Hershey's version, which differs materially (3/4 c peanut butter, 1/3 + 1/3 c sugars, 1 1/2 c flour) -- I checked hersheyland.com and rejected it. Family text's return-to-oven step for the kiss is a house addition.

name: Peanut Butter Cookies
flags: No source recorded. Family version is a small, distinctive formula (1/4 c butter only, 1/2 c peanut butter, 1/2 + 1/2 c sugars, 1 egg, just 1 cup flour, 1 t soda, no fork-crosshatch step). No published recipe with that butter-to-flour ratio surfaced; the well-known versions (Betty Crocker, Sally's, Handle the Heat) all use far more butter and flour. Not attaching a generic one.

name: Peanut Butter Pie
flags: Family source (Barb Cencula). Searching her name with the recipe returns nothing but unrelated published peanut butter pies.

name: Pepper Steak
flags: No source recorded. This is steak au poivre finished with bourbon -- the family version is unusually spare (bourbon and 2 T water deglaze, no cream, no stock, no shallot), which rules out the popular bourbon-peppercorn-cream versions (Food Network/Lomonaco, Charleston Magazine, etc.). Reads like a Craig Claiborne or similar mid-century newspaper recipe but I could not locate it. Note also that 'Pepper Steak' online overwhelmingly returns the Chinese-American beef-and-bell-pepper stir fry, which is a different dish entirely.

name: Petite Cheesecakes
flags: Attributed to Pat Willingham -- a personal/community-cookbook source. 'Petite Cheesecakes' is a common community-cookbook title (cooks.com carries two under that exact name) and the vanilla-wafer-in-a-cupcake-liner method is ubiquitous, so a same-named page would be a coincidence, not a source. Deliberately not attached.

name: Pickled Mushrooms
flags: Family source (Jan Symmes). Confirming search returned only unrelated published pickled mushroom recipes.

name: Plain Pastry for Pie Crust
headnote: A member transcription, credited to Better Homes and Gardens, of the standard all-shortening double-crust pastry. Flour and salt are cut with shortening to pea-size pieces, then ice water is sprinkled a tablespoon at a time over one section of the mixture, tossed with a fork and pushed aside before the next addition. Adding the water in that piecemeal way is what keeps the dough from being overworked in any one spot, which is where toughness comes from.
flags: LOW CONFIDENCE, flagged for human review. The family entry records no source at all, but its directions are near-verbatim Better Homes and Gardens New Cook Book 'Plain Pastry' wording ('For extra-tender pastry, cut in the shortening until like cornmeal. Cut in remaining shortening until like small peas'), and the cook's note ('For one 8, 9, or 10 inch double-crust pie, one lattice top pie, or two single crust pie shells') is BH&G's own yield line. So the recipe identity is almost certainly BH&G Plain Pastry. What is weaker is this particular page: it lists 1/2 t salt and a flat 6 T water, where the family text has 1 t salt and 5-8 T water, so it is an imperfect transcription of the same recipe. No official BH&G page for Plain Pastry is online. Promote or replace at will.

name: Playdough
flags: Not a recipe with a publisher -- the standard cooked cream-of-tartar play dough, here at triple batch scale (3 c flour, 1 1/2 c salt, 6 t cream of tartar, 3 c water, 3 T oil). Hundreds of identical versions exist on craft blogs with no original source; attaching one would be arbitrary.

name: Popeye Drops (Spinach Balls)
flags: No source recorded; 'Popeye Drops' is a community-cookbook title. Checked the closest published candidate, food.com's Stove Top Spinach Balls, and rejected it: that version hydrates the stuffing mix with 1 2/3 c hot water and adds mushrooms and onion, whereas the family recipe explicitly says do not cook the stuffing mix and contains neither. Many other near-identical spinach ball recipes exist on cooks.com and justapinch with no shared origin.

name: Popovers
flags: No source recorded. A bare four-ingredient popover formula (1 c milk, 2 eggs, 1 T melted butter, 1 c flour, 1/4 t salt) that appears in essentially every general cookbook; no published page is identifiable as its origin.

name: Pork Sausage Jim Lahey
flags: Source is correctly recorded as Jim Lahey, My Pizza (2012), and the family text is a faithful transcription from the book, including the metric weights (3 g fennel, 500 g pork butt, 8 g ginger, 6 g salt). The book is not excerpted online for this recipe -- searches turn up reviews of My Pizza and unrelated homemade pizza sausage recipes, none of which use Lahey's distinctive fresh ginger. No citable page.

name: Pork Tenderloin Roll-Up
flags: Family source (Alan MacArthur). Confirming search returns only unrelated published stuffed/rolled pork tenderloin recipes.

name: Potatoes Anna
flags: Family source (Jan Symmes). Pommes Anna is a classic French dish with many published versions (Betty Crocker, RecipeTin Eats, The Kitchn, Food Network), but none is Jan's, and the collection records her as the source. Deliberately not attached -- a same-named classic is exactly the case where a wrong link would be worse than none.

name: Pumpkin Pie
flags: IDENTIFIED BUT NOT FETCHABLE. The family version -- 1 (16 oz) can pumpkin, 1 (14 oz) can SWEETENED CONDENSED milk, 2 eggs, 1 t cinnamon, 1/2 t ginger, 1/2 t nutmeg, 1/2 t salt, bake 425F for 15 min then 350F for 35 -- is the Eagle Brand 'Perfect Pumpkin Pie', which is the condensed-milk pumpkin pie that circulated alongside Libby's canned pumpkin (hence the recorded source 'Libby'). Recommended URL for a human to verify and promote: https://www.eaglebrand.com/recipe/perfect-pumpkin-pie/ -- it returned HTTP 403 on fetch, so I could not confirm it or pull a digest, and per instruction I did not attempt any other route to that page. Separately I checked and REJECTED https://www.bigbearswife.com/1950s-libbys-old-pumpkin-pie-recipe/ : that is the pre-2019 Libby's can recipe, which uses 3/4 c sugar and EVAPORATED milk -- precisely the version the family's own cook's note distinguishes theirs from.

name: Raspberry Sauce
flags: Family source (Jan Symmes). Confirming search returned only unrelated published raspberry dessert sauces.

name: Rhubarb-Raspberry Pie (or Strawberry)
flags: Source recorded as Sunset, 1991. Found and REJECTED the obvious candidate, https://sunset.com/recipe/moms-raspberry-rhubarb-pie (James Carrier, Sunset, 2008): it thickens with 1/4 cup CORNSTARCH not quick-cooking tapioca, uses 3 1/2 c raspberries to 3 1/2 c rhubarb rather than the family's 4 c rhubarb to 1 c berries, bakes at 375F for 70-90 min rather than 400F for 40-50, and has no lemon juice. Same magazine, different recipe. Sunset's 1991 archive is not online.

name: Rib Roast Beef Recipe--from The Prime Choice--the one we use
flags: 'The Prime Choice' appears to be a butcher shop or meat purveyor whose cooking card the family kept (the method is the distinctive 550F sear for 10 minutes then 250F to 130-135F internal, with garlic powder forced into the fat cap and Worcestershire rubbed in). Searched for that business's instructions and for the method; nothing matching turned up. Many prime rib pages use a high-heat-then-low method but none is this card.

name: Rice Krispie Treats
headnote: Kellogg's own page for the treats, presented as the three-ingredient original that has been on the box for generations. Butter and marshmallows are melted together over low heat before the cereal goes in, so every grain gets coated while the marshmallow is still fluid; the mixture is then pressed into a buttered 13x9 pan with a buttered spatula or wax paper, which is what keeps it from sticking to everything.
comment_digest: No reader comments. Kellogg's own guidance: use fresh marshmallows for the best texture, serve the same day, and store airtight for up to two days at room temperature or up to six weeks frozen with wax paper between layers.
flags: Matches the family text exactly -- 3 T butter, 10 oz marshmallows (40 large or the mini equivalent), 6 cups Rice Krispies, melt over low heat, press into a 13x9x2 pan with wax paper or a buttered spatula. Recorded source is 'Rice Krispie Box', and this is that box recipe on the brand's site. Only drift: the box now says 5 1/2 cups minis where the family card says 4 cups.

name: RO-TEL Cheese Dip and Spread
headnote: The brand's page for the two-ingredient queso that made Ro-Tel a pantry staple: undrained Ro-Tel tomatoes and green chiles melted into cubed Velveeta over medium heat, about five minutes, or microwaved for the same time with a stir partway. Cubing the cheese and leaving the tomato liquid in is what lets it come together smooth instead of breaking or seizing. It is pitched as party and Tex-Mex food, served warm with chips, crackers or vegetables.
flags: Same dip, but the family text is the OLDER can-label version credited to Elsa Canning Co. (Ro-Tel's original Elsa, Texas canner), written at half scale -- 1/2 can Ro-Tel to 1/2 lb pasteurized cheese melted in a double boiler -- and it carries a long list of uses the brand no longer prints (spread on toast or hamburger buns, filling for hard-boiled eggs or celery, poured over corn chips). The linked page is the modern brand descendant at exactly double the quantities (10 oz can to 16 oz Velveeta). Marked medium because the specific Elsa Canning Co. label text is not online. Runner-up with the vintage history written up: https://www.deepsouthdish.com/2008/12/original-ro-tel-famous-queso-dip.html

name: Roast Chicken With Mustard Vinaigrette
headnote: A transcription of the Bon Appetit recipe, which the page itself credits to the May 1994 issue. A whole roasting chicken is stuffed with shallot and whole rosemary and sage sprigs, and mustard vinaigrette is worked under the breast skin as well as brushed over the outside. Starting at 450F for twenty minutes sets the skin, then dropping to 375F for the remaining hour and twenty lets the bird cook through without the herb-and-mustard coating burning; the reserved vinaigrette is served alongside.
flags: Page states the source as Bon Appetit, May 1994, which matches the collection's recorded source exactly, and the method and temperatures match the family text step for step (450F/20 min, 375F/1 hr 20, vinaigrette under the skin, cool 1 hour, can be made a day ahead). BigOven is an aggregator rather than the publisher, and it omits the accompanying Mustard Vinaigrette sub-recipe that the family text preserves. Runner-up: https://www.marga.org/foodblog/2011/01/roast-chicken-with-mustard-vinaigrette/

name: Roasted Asparagus with Mustard Vinaigrette
flags: No source recorded and the family text is a sketch rather than a formal recipe (a bunch of asparagus, roast at 425 for 10-15 min, and a three-ingredient dressing of Dijon, lemon juice and olive oil written as 'whisk together / add and whisk'). Nothing identifiable to attach.

name: Roasted Cauliflower with Garlic
flags: Source recorded as Epicurious, and the family text has the marks of an Epicurious/Gourmet party-size recipe (6 lbs cauliflower / 3 heads, 1/2 c olive oil, 4 garlic cloves, 425F for 25-30 min). epicurious.com returned SITE_BLOCKED on fetch, so I could not locate or verify the specific page and, per instruction, did not attempt any other route to it. Web search alone did not surface the Epicurious page among the many unrelated roasted-cauliflower recipes. Worth a human retry directly on epicurious.com.

name: Rolled Onion Sandwich
flags: No source recorded. A vintage bread-pinwheel appetizer with an unusual cooked brown-sugar/vinegar/egg-yolk dressing alongside cream cheese, green pepper and onion. Nothing published matches; the well-known 'onion sandwich' references (James Beard's, the Southern rolled variety) are different recipes.

name: Rosemary Pork and Mushrooms with Shallots
headnote: Posted by food.com member BeckyF as a slow-cooker supper that reminded her of her mother's cooking. Pork shoulder is cut into half-inch slices and browned first, then the fat is drained off before everything goes into the cooker, which is what keeps the finished braise from turning greasy over eight hours. Shallots, mushrooms, rosemary and a can of diced tomatoes supply all the liquid the pot needs.
comment_digest: The recurring correction is that the rosemary is underdosed -- several cooks doubled or tripled it, and some used whole sprigs instead of chopped. Other repeat additions are garlic powder, Worcestershire, a bay leaf and extra mushrooms. It is commonly served over rice or egg noodles.
flags: Ingredient list and method match the family text line for line, including the 1 T oil, 1 c chopped shallots, 2 lbs boneless pork shoulder in 1/2-inch slices, 2 c mushrooms, 1 T fresh rosemary, 1 t each salt and pepper, and one 14 oz can diced tomatoes, low 8 hours or high 4. The family copy also carries 'Recommended Unit Size: 3-6 Quarts', which is Crock-Pot brand cookbook boilerplate and matches the recorded source; the food.com posting is the same recipe without that line. Note the title on food.com is prefixed 'Crock Pot'.
